name: Time-restricted feeding

lead: Time-restricted feeding (TRF) means confining all eating to a set window each day, commonly 8 hours (16:8) but ranging from 6 to 12, and fasting for the rest. It does not specify what to eat. In looksmaxxing circles it is used as a simple way to lower body fat, which tends to reveal facial structure such as the jawline and cheekbones and improve muscle definition.

Human trials of daily eating windows have reported weight loss, lower blood pressure and improved insulin sensitivity in several populations, and reviews generally find results comparable to ordinary calorie restriction. Studies in resistance-trained men have examined whether lifters can keep strength and muscle on a 16/8 pattern.

paras: Practitioners pick a daily window, often late morning to evening or an early-day window, and take only calorie-free drinks outside it. Lifters on forums such as T Nation describe fitting their usual meals, or a bulk or cut plan, inside the window and say it simplifies tracking. People commonly report adjusting over a few weeks, and results follow whatever change in total intake occurs.

Short-term effects reported in reviews include hunger, irritability, headaches and dizziness, which often fade within a month. Health bodies advise against intermittent fasting patterns for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children, adolescents and people with or vulnerable to eating disorders, and people with insulin-dependent diabetes are advised to involve a doctor. Fitting enough protein and calories into a short window can be harder for people trying to gain muscle.

angle.text: TRF gives people a simple rule that can lower overall intake, and fat loss is what shows structure in the face and physique. Lifters also use it to organise cuts and bulks around a set window.

lead: Time-restricted feeding (TRF), also called time-restricted eating, is a form of intermittent fasting in which all food is eaten within a consistent daily window, usually between 6 and 12 hours, with the remainder of the day spent fasting. A popular version is 16:8 (16 hours fasting, 8 hours eating). Unlike calorie counting, it sets when rather than how much to eat. [1][2][3]

People pursuing a better look use TRF mainly as a route to lower body fat. Leaner faces show more jaw, cheekbone and under-eye structure, and leaner bodies show more muscle definition; some lifters also use it as a way to manage a cut or bulk with a fixed eating schedule. Forum users report that the window makes it easier to stay within a calorie target. [4][5]

Human trials of TRF have reported reductions in weight and blood pressure and improvements in insulin sensitivity, including a supervised feeding study in men with prediabetes in which benefits appeared even without weight loss. [6][7][8] The concept grew from rodent research showing that mice restricted to an 8-hour feeding window were protected from diet-induced obesity. [9]
infobox: 6 to 12 hours of eating per day (16:8 common)

paras: TRF restricts the daily eating period without necessarily changing what is eaten. Variants include early TRF, where the window ends in the afternoon to align with circadian rhythms, and mid-day or late windows. [10][11] Other intermittent fasting schedules, such as alternate-day fasting and the 5:2 diet, restrict whole days instead. [2][3]

Forum posts show TRF being suggested to lifters trying to lean out, with advice to simply compress usual meals into the window. [4][5] Some posters describe it as meal spacing combined with large protein servings. [12] Others on the same forum argue that evidence is strongest for early-day windows and that other variants are adaptations beyond the research. [13]
Questions that recur include how many calories break a fast and whether lifters can eat enough in a short window to gain muscle. [14][13]

Researchers propose that aligning eating with the body's circadian rhythm, and extending the nightly fast, shifts metabolism toward fat-derived ketones and improves glucose handling. [2][15][16] A 2016 Science review describes how feeding and fasting cycles interact with clock genes that regulate metabolism. [15] Rodent studies also report effects on the gut microbiome and on fat-cell thermogenesis. [17][18]

A 2017 review of intermittent fasting concluded that modified fasting regimens appear to promote weight loss and may improve metabolic health, and that reducing nighttime eating may help. [1] A Canadian systematic review covering 27 trials in people with overweight or obesity reported weight loss with intermittent fasting. [6] A 2022 review described comparable benefits across alternate-day fasting and TRF. [2]

A supervised feeding trial in men with prediabetes tested early TRF while keeping weight stable and reported better insulin sensitivity, blood pressure and oxidative stress. [7] A five-week randomised trial compared early and mid-day TRF in healthy people without obesity. [8] A trial in patients with metabolic syndrome tested a 10-hour window and reported weight, blood pressure and lipid changes. [10] A controlled study compared daytime with delayed eating on weight and metabolism. [11]

In resistance-trained men, an eight-week 16/8 trial measured basal metabolism, strength, body composition, inflammation and cardiovascular risk factors. [16] Wikipedia's overview notes that intermittent fasting does not appear to improve athletic performance and that evidence for TRF specifically is preliminary. [3]

Short-term side effects include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea and headaches, usually fading within a month. [3] Intermittent fasting is not recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children, adolescents, or people with or vulnerable to eating disorders, and some health authorities advise medical consultation for people with diabetes. [3] The US National Institute on Aging does not recommend it for the general public, and dropout rates in trials range widely. [3]

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums, TRF is discussed as a practical way for lifters to run cuts and bulks, with debate over which window is best. [13][19]
